analysis.one_liner: Removes the insurance industry's exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing and monopolies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee after being referred there in May 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, insurance companies have been exempt from federal antitrust laws under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, meaning they generally cannot be sued for price fixing, dividing up markets, or monopolizing the way other businesses can. This bill would strip that exemption for four kinds of conduct: fixing prices, agreeing with competitors on who sells insurance where, forcing customers to buy one insurance product to get another, and monopolizing part of the insurance business. It would keep the exemption for routine data sharing, like pooling historical claims statistics and standard actuarial calculations, which insurers use to price policies accurately. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and businesses that buy insurance. If insurers could be sued for colluding on prices, dividing territories, or tying products together, competition would likely put downward pressure on premiums for auto, home, health, and business insurance. Honest insurers that compete on price would also benefit from a level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that insurance companies engaging in price fixing, market allocation, unlawful tying arrangements, or monopolization can be prosecuted under federal antitrust laws, including Federal Trade Commission enforcement [S2][S3].

It preserves the antitrust exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data, determining loss development factors, and performing actuarial services, so insurers can still pool the statistical information needed to price policies without facing liability [S2][S3].

It gives smaller insurers a longer transition period (four years versus two) before the trend-factor exemption expires, and permanently spares very small insurers from liability for joint trend-factor determinations [S3].
The bill takes effect one year after enactment, giving insurers time to adjust their pricing practices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would lose the ability to fix prices, divide markets, and tie products together without antitrust liability, and would face legal costs and potentially lower premiums as a result. Any cost savings to insurers from industry-wide coordinated pricing would end.

drawbacks.text: Critics of repealing the McCarran-Ferguson exemption argue that joint industry sharing of claims and pricing data, even when limited to statistics, can blur into coordinated pricing, and that antitrust lawsuits against insurers could raise legal costs that get passed to policyholders. This bill tries to address that by expressly exempting statistical data sharing and actuarial work, but any line between data pooling and price coordination is litigated case by case [S2][S3].

The bill still leaves most of the antitrust exemption intact: insurance conduct outside the four listed categories remains exempt from federal antitrust law, and state-regulated insurance activity is untouched [S3].
The bill was narrow in scope and sponsor support was modest: six cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support, which limited its prospects even before the committee considered it [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: making insurance companies follow the same antitrust rules as nearly every other business, which would allow enforcement against outright collusion on price and territory. The bill was carefully drafted to protect legitimate joint statistical work that insurers genuinely need, and to phase in over two to four years so pricing systems could adjust. The main honest limitation is that it targets only four categories of conduct and leaves the broader exemption in place for everything else, so its practical effect on premiums depends heavily on how much hidden price coordination actually existed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on May 17, 2005, with five Democratic cosponsors joining as original sponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the chamber's first step for most legislation [S5].

No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup or hearing on the bill, the House never debated it, and no vote was ever scheduled before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The insurance industry is better off, because the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption it has operated under since 1945 remains fully intact, keeping insurers shielded from antitrust suits for price fixing, market allocation, and monopolization that other industries face.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Insurance Competitive Pricing Act of 2005 and served as its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Brian Baird, Donna Christensen, Joseph Crowley, Maurice Hinchey, and Gene Taylor
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee of referral; chair controlled the agenda
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 17, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on [S4]; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record of party positions exists.

industries.note: The bill would strip the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption for price fixing, dividing markets, tying products, and monopolizing, exposing insurers to antitrust suits and enforcement they have been shielded from since 1945. The industry's shielded pricing power comes at the cost of higher premiums for policyholders.

industries.industry: Insurance data, actuarial, and statistical bureaus
industries.note: The bill expressly keeps the antitrust exemption for collecting and sharing historical loss data, loss development factors, actuarial services, and (temporarily) trend factors, so the industry's joint statistical infrastructure survives intact.
